title: Econ scan: hosting mix & budget constraints - Reckon Finance discovery
topics: hosted vs dedicated vs private tradeoffs
next steps for pricing scenarios and benchmark
summary: Discovery for Reckon Finance to understand unit cost sensitivity and hosting mix given a $15k monthly inference budget. Discussed current usage (~50M tokens/month), latency targets, batching and caching levers, viability of a dedicated reserved pool vs hosted API versus VPC/private, and security/compliance requirements. Agreed to run a short pilot and deliver three pricing scenarios (hosted, dedicated committed, private baseline) plus a lightweight perf benchmark for their 512-token average completions.
next_steps: Mia to send three pricing scenarios and a short pilot proposal by 2026-08-18
Omar to propose benchmark test harness and required sample prompts by 2026-08-20
Reckon to confirm pilot approval & security contacts (infosec) by 2026-08-21
action_items: Mia Carter - send hosted / committed / private price comparison spreadsheet (due 2026-08-18)
Omar Li - draft benchmark plan and simple load script plus sample prompt set (due 2026-08-20)
Tara Chen - share real traffic histogram and 95p latency SLO target (due 2026-08-18)
Samir Patel - provide infra/security contacts for VPC/KMS questions (due 2026-08-21)
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-08-14 16:00 PDT
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Mia Carter (Redwood AE), Omar Li (Redwood SE), Tara Chen (Reckon Head of ML), Samir Patel (Platform Eng), Lena Ortiz (Finance)

Auto-summary: quick econ scan - identify which hosting mix fits Reckon's $15k/mo budget for inference and what pilot size makes sense. Security touchpoints: SOC2, SSO, KMS + residency.

---
[00:00] Mia Carter: hey everyone thanks for joining, i'm Mia from Redwood, joining me is Omar our solutions engineer — quick intros?
[00:12] Tara Chen: hi Tara, head of ML at Reckon, focusing on customer support automation and risk scoring.
[00:18] Samir Patel: Samir, platform eng, i'll be owning infra conversations.
[00:22] Lena Ortiz: Lena, finance, i'll be watching the budget. hello.
[00:28] Omar Li: great, quick agenda: usage today, target SLOs, levers (batching, caching, quant), hosting options, and next steps, ok?
[00:37] Tara Chen: yup, go ahead.

[03:05] Mia Carter: to set context, you mentioned a rough budget of $15k per month for inference, is that firm or a starting point?
[03:12] Lena Ortiz: that's our current target envelope for the next quarter — could be flexible up a bit if benefit is clear but we need to justify to finance.
[03:30] Samir Patel: also important — we prefer not to manage full infra if hosted option gives parity on latency and cost. but private is on the table for PII data.

[05:02] Omar Li: can you share current traffic? Tara?
[05:10] Tara Chen: sure; current pre-prod usage is about 50 million tokens a month across two apps; peaks are ~200k reqs/day, avg request = ~120 tokens including context + completion, and p95 latency desire is ~300-400ms for shorter interactions.
[05:28] Omar Li: okay so ballpark per-request tokens 120, 50M tokens/month, at 120 tokens/request => roughly 416k requests/month.
[05:45] Lena Ortiz: yep math checks out.

[07:10] Mia Carter: quick note on levers — batching can reduce per-token compute by sharing attention work across simultaneous requests, prefix caching (we call it KV cache sometimes) can avoid regenerating system prompts for chat-style flows. quantization and model selection also change unit cost.
[07:33] Tara Chen: when you say KV cache, do you mean we can keep the user's long history cached? that's important for our support assistant.
[07:40] Omar Li: yeah, you can cache KV up to the session window — avoids repeating forward pass for earlier tokens. in practice for chat that'll lower token generation by 20-40% depending on reuse.
[07:55] Samir Patel: small note, we have retention rules — PII must be redacted before being stored or we need private hosting with KMS.

[10:00] Mia Carter: for hosting mix options: 1) Hosted API - simplest, pay per use, quick to pilot. 2) Dedicated - reserved capacity for predictable throughput and lower unit cost with commits. 3) Private/VPC on-prem - full control for compliance, higher setup and baseline cost.
[10:18] Lena Ortiz: can you give an example of unit economics across those? simple numbers to compare.

[12:02] Omar Li: sure so illustrative only: hosted per-token gen cost X, after batching and cache usually you see 20-35% savings. committed dedicated may reduce unit compute by another 15-30% depending on commit size. private has similar runtime cost but you take infra ops + license overhead.
[12:25] Tara Chen: what is X in that example?
[12:30] Omar Li: we typically show customers a hosted baseline then two commit tiers. for this conversation think of hosted baseline at say $0.0009 per generation token (this is illustrative) — which for 50M tokens is ~$45k/month raw. but with caching + batching that can drop to around $27k-$32k. a dedicated committed profile with a medium monthly commit might land at $16k-$20k depending on utilization.
[12:59] Lena Ortiz: that's a big delta from $45k to possibly $16k.
[13:05] Mia Carter: yep that's why we run sensitivity analyses — small changes in batching, token counts, or commit utilization swing the unit cost a lot.

[15:22] Samir Patel: question — in dedicated commits do we still get fallbacks to hosted if we hit spikes? we need reliability for bursts.
[15:30] Omar Li: yes, you can configure routing/fallback policies — commit first then hosted as overflow. that does cause some accounting complexity but we can show blended estimates.

[18:00] Tara Chen: our main unknown is how much caching will help in the support assistant — many requests repeat templates and system prompts. can you model that?
[18:12] Omar Li: we can, if you can share a sample of session traces or a prompt set. even a small corpus helps to model expected token-reuse and estimate savings from prefix/KV caching.
[18:30] Tara Chen: we'll redact customer PII and share example sequences.

[21:40] Mia Carter: Lena, from finance perspective, is runway more important than exact per-token low cost? e.g., are you more comfortable with predictable monthly commit vs variable hosted spend?
[21:52] Lena Ortiz: predictable is preferred — easier to plan. a reserve is attractive if we expect steady usage. but commit is a commitment — we need proof via a pilot.

[24:10] Omar Li: recommended pilot: 4-week run using hosted plus a small dedicated commit to simulate committed utilization (we can use spot reserved equivalents) and run benchmark for latency and unit cost. we'll instrument token-level cost and token reduction from cache.
[24:28] Samir Patel: how invasive is private deploy for us? we use AWS, have VPC controls and KMS already.
[24:36] Omar Li: private is typically a few weeks of setup: VPC peering, deploy private control plane, integrate customer KMS for keys. extra lead time if you need air-gapped on-prem.

[27:00] Lena Ortiz: we also need SOC2 and audit logs — how does Redwood handle L4 audit / retention?
[27:10] Mia Carter: Redwood has SOC2 Type II and can surface audit logs per request, and has KMS integration for private — we can send security package after this call.
[27:20] Tara Chen: perfect, continue.

[30:05] Omar Li: let's run through a quick worked example using your numbers: 50M tokens/month baseline. if baseline hosted rate is illustrative $0.0009/token => $45k. assume we get 30% saving from KV caching and batching => $31.5k. now if you take a dedicated commit at 70% utilization that might drop to $17k-$18k all-in. the key is utilization and the initial commit size.
[30:45] Samir Patel: what counts as utilization? peak vs average?
[30:50] Omar Li: utilization in a dedicated pool is the percent of GPU time used relative to reserved capacity across the billing period. we model it on average throughput. spikes are handled by overflow to hosted.

[33:11] Mia Carter: quick clarification — when we quote dedicated numbers we include estimated SW overhead and some margin for kernel efficiency. exact savings depend on model and sequence length distribution.
[33:25] Tara Chen: can you do that math for our higher-complexity risk-scoring flows? those are longer sequences — like 512 tokens.
[33:34] Omar Li: longer sequences increase per-token compute and thus change break-even points; dedicated helps more with long sequences because batching is less effective across long sequences but dedicated kernel selection and memory layout optimize those better. we'll put a 512-token scenario in the spreadsheet.

[36:05] Samir Patel: security nuance — we encrypt payloads to KMS but don't want customer data retained by Redwood in hosted mode. is that an option?
[36:13] Mia Carter: hosted with no retention or short retention is possible — we can disable retention or set short TTLs for logs, but if you have regulatory needs around raw data not leaving your VPC, private is safer. we'll document retention knobs.

[39:00] Lena Ortiz: for finance, can you show a blended cost projection with three rows: hosted baseline, hosted+optimizations, and committed/dedicated? with sensitivity +/-20% tokens?
[39:13] Mia Carter: yes that's exactly what we'll send in the scenario spreadsheet.

[42:20] Omar Li: quick tech note: prefix/KV caching effectiveness depends on session reuse. if your support flows repeat the same system prompt 60-70% of the time we often see savings in the 25-40% range. quantization also can shave runtime cost but with small quality tradeoffs.
[42:45] Tara Chen: quality tradeoffs are a concern for risk scoring — can't drop quality. so we'd prefer batching/caching and commit before quant.
[43:00] Omar Li: makes sense. for risk scoring we usually recommend compute-optimized configs with minimal quantization.

[46:30] Samir Patel: about pilot infra: can we run a smoke test in our staging VPC to measure KV cache benefit without full private deploy?
[46:40] Omar Li: yes — we can run a hosted test instrumented with session traces and simulate a VPC-like network path. or we can spin up a short private evaluation with VPC peering for 2-3 weeks if you want the production network fidelity.

[49:10] Tara Chen: timeline — we want results before next finance review on Aug 28th. is that feasible?
[49:18] Mia Carter: yes if we start immediately we can do a 2-3 week pilot and deliver numbers by Aug 26th.

[52:05] Lena Ortiz: what's the minimum commit we should consider to see meaningful unit cost improvement?
[52:12] Omar Li: typically a small commit tier shows modest gains; meaningful break-even for you likely starts at a commit that covers ~50-60% of your baseline throughput — for 50M tokens that maps to roughly the mid-tier commit. we'll calculate exact tokens->GPU-hours in the spreadsheet.

[55:00] Mia Carter: ok recap: 1) we'll send three scenario spreadsheets (hosted baseline, hosted+optimizations, dedicated commit) 2) Omar will share benchmark plan and simple scripts and request sample prompts/traces 3) Reckon to share redacted traces and confirm infosec contact 4) agree to target pilot results by Aug 26.
[55:25] Samir Patel: sounds good.
[55:30] Tara Chen: one more thing — does Redwood provide chargeback reporting per route? we need per-team visibility.
[55:38] Omar Li: yes console provides per-route per-model token breakdowns, token-level cost attribution and can export to your billing system.

[58:00] Lena Ortiz: ok i'll be the finance reviewer, please include a simple monthly P&L slide that shows delta vs our $15k target so i can present it.
[58:12] Mia Carter: will do.

[60:15] Tara Chen: thanks all, excited to see the scenarios.
[60:20] Mia Carter: thanks everyone, we'll follow up via email with the spreadsheet and pilot plan.
[60:30] [call ends]
